paper_title: Can We Edit LLMs for Long-Tail Biomedical Knowledge
caption_used: The performance of knowledge probing after editing with different editing methods on BioMedLM, where "Base" denotes LLM without editing. The x-axis shows co-occurrence number on a logarithmic scale, while the y-axis represents accuracy (ACC %). All six methods show improving accuracy with increasing co-occurrence frequency. ROME consistently achieves the highest accuracy, starting at approximately 51% and reaching roughly 66% at the highest co-occurrence numbers. MEND and MEMIT follow as the next best performers, with MEND reaching approximately 56% and MEMIT approximately 55%. Notably, IKE demonstrates a steeper improvement rate than FT, surpassing it at co-occurrence numbers above 10^2 to reach approximately 52% at the highest frequency. The Base model exhibits the lowest performance throughout, plateauing at approximately 44%.
model_annotation: The plot illustrates the accuracy (ACC %) of knowledge probing after applying different editing methods to the BioMedLM model, with the x-axis representing co-occurrence number on a logarithmic scale ranging from 0 to 10^3, and the y-axis showing accuracy from 40% to 65% in increments of 5%. The six methods compared are Base (black circles), MEND (brown diamonds), FT (blue triangles), MEMIT (purple squares), IKE (red triangles), and ROME (green squares). All methods show increasing accuracy as co-occurrence number increases. ROME consistently achieves the highest accuracy, starting at approximately 51% at the lowest co-occurrence and rising to about 66% at 10^3. MEND and MEMIT follow, with MEND reaching approximately 56% and MEMIT approximately 55% at the highest co-occurrence. IKE shows a steeper improvement than FT, surpassing it around 10^2 and reaching approximately 52% at 10^3, while FT reaches about 48%. The Base model, representing the unedited LLM, exhibits the lowest accuracy throughout, starting at about 39% and plateauing at approximately 44% by 10^3.
